extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, media-relations managers, and PR students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for planning, executing, evaluating press events (conferences, parties, press rooms) and for using radio formats (paid spots, PSAs, talk shows) as part of public relations programs. Includes logistical, ethical, audience-targeting, and evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose press conference vs. news release
rubrics_metrics.description: Catering to the press—housing, feeding, and petting—is only an occasional task... both sides find it easier to depend on news releases for transmitting routine information. The press conference should be used when it is clear that giving the press an opportunity to question expert sources will result in more meaningful and effective news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use news releases for routine information; use a press conference when reporters' ability to question experts will improve coverage or when dialogue is needed. Avoid conferences when a release suffices (reporters may not show up) or when the news value is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use press parties only for genuine reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The press party, festive cousin to the news conference, is appropriate when an organization has genuine reason to mark some sort of milestone, such as an anniversary, or when the attendance of celebrities is a cause for excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve social press events for legitimate celebrations or when star power provides clear news/visual interest; avoid socializing that could be perceived as trying to buy coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh potential miscues before proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many ways for a press event to turn into a disaster. The news value may be so weak that the reporters feel duped. The release announcing the news conference may contain all the information the press needs, so reporters don’t show up... The guest or interviewee may not perform as expected... The timing may be wrong, or a breaking news event may preempt the attention of the press. The broadcast press, with its lights and microphones, may sour the print press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before committing resources, assess news value, whether advance materials already satisfy reporters, guest preparedness, timing relative to other events, and potential conflicts between broadcast and print needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply PR management models appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Although used in all four models of public relations, press conferences and similar events work especially well in the two-way symmetric model. Be careful if you use press events for press agentry or two-way asymmetric purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your goal is dialogue (two-way symmetric), press events are appropriate. If the goal is controlling information (press agentry/asymmetric), use caution—attempts at control may alienate the press and cause adverse publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic objectives for press events
rubrics_metrics.description: With press releases, your objectives are communication (placing a story on the media agenda) and retention of the message. With press events, you have little control over the retention objective because somebody else writes the story. Your objective, therefore, should be to get your organization’s point of view on the media agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to place your POV on the media agenda and monitor accuracy of coverage; avoid attempting to force reporters to accept or evaluate your position favorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select press events for appropriate programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Press events can be used in general media relations, when the organization has news of consequence or wide interest to the public... Press events can be held to announce policy positions in public affairs and government relations programs and to meet with media serving activist publics. They can be called to release financial information. Specialists in promotion frequently use press events to publicize new automobile lines, sports events, or fund-raising drives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use events for matters of consequence/wide interest, public-affairs announcements, financial disclosures, promotions, and where the medium's needs are matched to the message. In smaller communities, prefer individual reporter contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match content to publics' involvement level
rubrics_metrics.description: Press events can be used for media that serve both high- and low-involvement publics. Be careful not to mix the two at the same time, however. Detailed, technical information will be necessary for the trade press or media serving activist publics. Simplified information will be needed for general assignment reporters worked for the mass (low-involvement) media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment attendees by interest/technical level; prepare separate materials or sessions for trade/activist press versus general assignment reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and schedule press events carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Press events cost more than press releases. You must rent a room, buy refreshments, and rent equipment. So be sure to budget for those items... Press events also require careful timing. Devices such as Gantt and PERT diagrams can be especially useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include room rental, catering, AV, and staffing in the budget; use project planning tools to coordinate timing and logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate events by coverage and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate a press event by determining whether it resulted in increased press coverage of your organization, and by the accuracy of that coverage. You can measure both effects by content-analyzing press clippings... When possible, ask reporters for formal or informal reaction to your press event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use content analysis of clippings and reporter feedback; recognize you control attendance and facilitation more than final stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite the right reporters/editors by beat
rubrics_metrics.description: If we send an invitation or release to the managing editor or the city editor, a general-assignment reporter might be sent to the event... It’s far wiser to invite business editors if our story involves economics, political writers if we are involved in a legislative matter, the entertainment columnist if we are sponsoring a cultural event...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target invitations to beat editors/reporters who will best cover the topic rather than relying on generic editor contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide scope of invite list (reporters vs. editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shall we invite bona fide reporters only, or a wider list of journalists? If the story has legitimate spot news interest, the presence of press hangers-on may interfere... On the other hand, if our news conference is intended to suggest a continuing story that deserves prolonged coverage, it may be wise to invite managing editors and editorial writers...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the need for immediate reporting against the goal of influencing long-term news agendas when deciding who to invite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage print vs. broadcast attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Should print and broadcast press be invited to the same conference? If so, how can we assure that both are adequately served? Early morning and late afternoon are good times for the print press, but midday usually is better for television... if television crews arrive in full force... the print press may be pushed to the side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider separate or split conferences (segments) for TV and print, schedule times to suit each medium, and plan staging to avoid marginalizing one group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent embarrassing silences and keep Q&A flowing
rubrics_metrics.description: A news conference may be jeopardized if no reporter is willing to ask the opening question... Some organizations routinely seat one or two members of their own public relations staff or the editor of the organization's magazine with the working press to raise additional questions at the appropriate time... It probably is better to prepare your speaker to raise and answer his own questions if the press is remiss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have contingency plans for Q&A: prepare speaker to self-initiate discussion, position knowledgeable staff to ask helpful questions (handled subtly), and train facilitators to keep momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and appoint qualified spokespersons
rubrics_metrics.description: If your organization provides a spokesperson who is not adequately prepared, or who does not know how to handle questions from the press, the conference quickly falls apart. Until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission appointed a qualified ‘point man’ to brief reporters covering the Three-Mile Island incident, the press complained of ‘conflicting and contradictory statements’...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and train a qualified, authorized spokesperson (a 'point man') who can provide clear, consistent information and handle difficult questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate reporters who refuse to attend or ask questions
rubrics_metrics.description: You must be prepared, too, for reporters who refuse to attend a press conference because... Some print reporters flatly refuse to raise questions while television cameras are running... If coverage by the reporters who complain is important to you, be prepared to make special arrangements so that they can interview your speaker or obtain the information in another manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer alternative interview times, separate access for print reporters, or one-on-one briefings as needed to secure desired coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and method of invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The only compromise seems to be sending out a press release (combined with an 'invitation' and an RSVP postal card, if you wish) about ten days before the event. Then, plan to call the editor the day before to confirm whether or not a reporter will be sent. Some PR practitioners... reverse the process, making the phone contact ten days ahead to alert the editor about the upcoming event, then timing the written reminder to arrive just a day or two ahead...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a two-step approach: advance notice (≈10 days) plus a day-before confirmation; adapt between written and phone contact based on individual editor preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect journalistic ethics when offering amenities
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing invitations to a press party or social event, special consideration should be given to the ethics codes... An important clause... states: 'Nothing of value shall be accepted.' This is generally interpreted to mean gifts having intrinsic value (but excluding premiums or mementos such as imprinted ball-point pens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gifts of intrinsic value, don't send invitations to reporters' private homes, be cautious about inviting spouses unless event norms justify it, and be sensitive to news organizations' policies about paying or hosting journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate venue (on-site vs. hotel vs. field)
rubrics_metrics.description: If your organization has a large boardroom, auditorium... you may be able to hold a press conference in your own facility—provided... you are located within a short drive of the media, and you have adequate parking available... hotels, motels, and restaurants frequently are used for press conferences, simply because they are centrally located...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select venue for convenience, visual interest (e.g., plant tours), parking/access, and facilities; consider bussing press to remote sites only if news value justifies inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect and confirm facility logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives of the PR department should make at least one on-site inspection... to check for items such as: adequate electrical outlets for audiovisual equipment; sufficient water pitchers and drinking glasses; ashtrays, and provisions for a nonsmoking section; phone booths outside the room; comfortable seating and, if appropriate, tables for writing or for displaying handouts and brochures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct pre-event walkthroughs with facility staff; ensure AV power, water, smoking accommodations, phone access (or temporary units), seating, display space, and signage to avoid confusion and distractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partition/noise problems; prepare signage
rubrics_metrics.description: One sure way to ruin the effect is to [use] half of a partitioned room, only to find that a hog-calling contest or a demonstration of stereo speakers has been scheduled for space on the other side of the flimsy partition... have your art department prepare plenty of signs pointing the way to the proper outside entrance, the conference room, the phones, and, of course, the rest rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rent the entire room when possible to ensure quiet; provide clear directional signage to streamline logistics for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide appropriate amenities for reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is never inappropriate to provide coffee and soft drinks, along with donuts and cookies... most news reporters carry their own paper and pencils, but it is useful to have a supply on hand... Radio people often wish to record a speech or presentation... arrange to have a single microphone leading not only to the public address system, but also to a box... where each journalist can 'jack in' to the sound source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer modest refreshments, supplies (paper, pencils), and audio arrangements that allow reporters to record without cluttering the speaker area; plan AV jacks/feeds and a designated spot for broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute helpful handouts strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer may be a combination of techniques: a one-page outline of material to be covered (placed on every chair), a selection of fact sheets (placed on the press table), and a text of the main speaker’s prepared statement (passed out at the door as reporters leave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise outlines in advance (on chairs), fact sheets centrally, and full statements upon exit to reduce disruptions and prevent early departures; station staff at door to track who receives materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set up a press/hospitality/working room
rubrics_metrics.description: Something called the 'hospitality room' frequently is set up... The working press room... the press expects the sponsor of the event... to set up a press room... space is rented from a hotel. Or arrangements may be made to use a public facility in order to set up a temporary news operation with links to the wire services and major media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a nearby hospitality room for informal contacts and a working press room with phones, typing equipment, and wire links for extended press operations; follow up informal chats with businesslike contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff the press room with knowledgeable PR personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a good idea to designate one or more members of the PR staff to be available in the press room regularly—holding briefings, providing background information... It is extremely important that knowledgeable members of the PR staff be assigned press-room duty, not just go-fers and clerks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign experienced staff with authority to expedite access to sources; ensure staff can provide timely, high-quality information and solve logistical problems for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up after the event
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully keep track of those who attend every event or press conference. Good records help you decide whom to invite to your next briefing... the next morning the staff should conduct a full review of the event's success or problems. A checklist with names of every member of the press should be maintained... Follow-up mailings should be ready to go within days, along with additional fact sheets in case of a developing news story...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain attendance lists, debrief staff the following day, send follow-up materials within days (fact sheets, photos, souvenirs if applicable), and monitor media for coverage to inform future invitations/strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use radio for local, repeatable, emergency messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio is another person talking to you. Radio is local. And the cost of radio is comparatively inexpensive per message, which permits an organization to repeat something until it sinks in... radio’s greatest attribute is utility in sudden or emergency situations when it is necessary to get a quickly prepared message to the general public or specialized publics on short notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage radio for frequent repetition, locality targeting, and urgent/emergency announcements; prepare concise, clear copy suitable for audio delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buy paid radio ads when precise control is required
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to dictate the precise content, time, and date of your message, you'll have to pay for advertising space. The size of your budget will determine what kinds of paid spots you can afford. It costs more to buy drive-time spots... than it does to buy late-night time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paid spots to control timing and content; budget for prime-time costs or accept less desirable placements for lower cost; consider package buys for repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit PSAs understanding scheduling limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to get their broadcast licenses renewed, commercial stations must demonstrate that they have provided the public service of distributing useful information... When the information is carried in the form of a free advertisement, it is known as a public-service announcement, or PSA... Usually only nonprofit groups may expect to get PSAs on the air... the organization that submits a PSA in any form should expect to hear it aired mainly in time periods when paid advertising cannot be sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonprofit groups can submit PSAs but should expect unfavorable time slots; provide multiple versions for variety and station flexibility; consider script submission, recorded spokesperson, or mailed polished spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Community Bulletin formats for local nonprofit listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Many stations offer a variation on the PSA, variously called 'Community Bulletin Board,' 'Around the Town,' or 'In (our town) Today'... Most stations limit the bulletin board to nonprofit organizations or to nonprofit events sponsored by businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For local events and community notices, submit concise copy to the station manager or news desk; these formats often provide an easy on-air listing for nonprofit activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt press materials for radio/newscast use and staged live events
rubrics_metrics.description: The press release, especially when it is geared to radio’s special needs, can gain you air time when you have a legitimate news story. The staged event is another way to create free news coverage...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write releases tailored for radio (concise, audio-friendly), and consider live staged events that produce visual/offbeat moments attractive to broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and participate in talk shows strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Many organizations assign at least one well-informed member to monitor each broadcast. That way, if the conversation turns to [subject]... an opportunity is provided to offer the group’s standard line... When topics are announced in advance, it may also be useful to assign members of your organization to join the ranks of the callers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign staff to monitor call-in/talk shows, prepare standard lines, arrange for knowledgeable spokespeople to appear as guests or callers, and use talk shows to respond to misinformation or advance organizational positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue public-affairs programming and deejay outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Most stations air two or three programs a week in which a member of the news staff... interviews a newsmaker... A call or letter to the station proposing a program or a segment usually will get a reply... Disk jockeys love to 'chat' with their listeners while changing records. Deejays need new material all of the time and often seize upon an unusual tidbit of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch program ideas or segments to stations (accepting late-night slots when necessary), and supply DJs with short, intriguing tidbits or local angles to prompt on-air mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of equal-time/fairness provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC’s Fairness Doctrine requires broadcast stations to offer the right of reply to anyone who has been criticized on the air. Under the personal-attack provision, the station must notify the person or persons of the right of reply and furnish them with a copy of the original script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor broadcasts for personal attacks or criticisms of your organization/clients; request and use right-of-reply provisions as necessary (note: historical/regulatory context may change—confirm current law/regulation).
